sections.title: Nature and Miracle
sections.html:
God created the world in such a way that, as a rule, He governs it through the way of nature, and at times through miracles. Nature operates within an ordered framework of laws that can be understood, whereas miracles break through the order of nature. The difference between nature and miracle exists only from the human perspective: the order of nature seems to a person self-evident and self-sustaining by virtue of the laws embedded in it, and therefore miracles impress him more, since they reveal the power of God that overcomes the order of nature. But from the perspective of the Creator there is no difference between them, for God gives life to everything, to nature and to miracle alike; by His will He established that the world should operate according to the laws of nature, and by His will He established that at times it should operate in a way that breaks through the laws, which we call a miracle. Therefore, what is called a miracle can also be called nature, in the sense that the governance through miracles also has an order that the Creator established (Maharal). Conversely, nature too can be considered a miracle, because it exists only by virtue of God's will; it is only that, from a superficial view, it seems that God governs the miracle openly and nature in a hidden way. Thus the governance of nature can be called hidden miracles, as we say in the prayer: 'Your miracles that are with us every day' (Ramban, Shemot 13:16).

With this in mind, let us look at the world again. God created the world with wisdom, that is, in such a way that it operates through laws, which are called the laws of nature. And God created man in the image of God, that is, with the ability to choose and to create, and thereby to influence his own life and the life of the whole world and to advance it toward its rectification (tikkun) and redemption. As a rule, the rectification and redemption of the world must take place through the way of nature, for in this way a person understands the laws by which the world operates, and knows that every action he takes has an influence on what will happen to him and to those around him. If he chooses to add good, he will add good to himself and to those around him; if he chooses evil, he will harm himself and those around him. If he learns a profession, he will be able to find work. If he works honestly and diligently, he will merit a good livelihood. If human beings develop science, they will merit greater prosperity. If a man respects, loves and gladdens his wife, and the wife acts likewise toward her husband, they will merit a good and happy life, and will be able to raise and educate their children properly. If he is good and loyal to his friends, he will merit good and supportive friends. Above this, if he studies Torah and fulfills its mitzvot, he will merit to express the image of God within him in the most excellent way, and will be a partner with God in advancing the world toward its rectification and redemption. Thus God created nature as the most suitable framework for revealing the power and talents of man.1

sections.title: The Deficiency in the Governance of Nature and the Need for Miracles
sections.html:
However, there is a deficiency in the governance of nature, in that it can cause the name of God to be forgotten, and miracles are intended to remedy this deficiency. The deficiency in the governance of nature can be described in three ways:

First, the laws of nature by which the world operates appear to a person so orderly and firm that it is as if their power were their own and they had no Creator who created them. And when the orders collapse, through miracles that break through the laws of nature, as well as through outbursts of the mighty forces of nature, such as lightning and thunder, earthquake and fire, the belief that there is One who created the world rises again into his consciousness (see Berakhot 59b).

Second, even when a person remembers that the world has a Creator, the wisdom and might in the laws of nature may cause him to think that since the Creation nature runs by itself, without God continuing to give it life and to watch over it. The implication arising from such a consciousness is that a person must fight for his survival while imprisoned within the laws of nature and within the coarse drives that rule him, without the ability to change himself and the world for the better. Therefore, God at times breaks through the boundaries of nature and performs miracles, and teaches human beings that it is He who sustains the laws of nature, in order to bestow His light and goodness on human beings through them. From this a person can understand that his role is to walk in the ways of God, to discover the hidden aspects of the laws of nature and to use them for good, and the more he discovers them, the more he will be able to make the world better.

Third, even righteous people who always remember that God created the world and governs it may forget that the nature in which they live is not perfect. They grow accustomed to the fact that the divine governance is hidden from the world, and many times the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper, and within this framework they try to do the very best according to the guidance of the Torah. Through the miracles, which come from a higher and more rectified world that will be revealed in the future, we remember our longings for the rectification of the world, refuse to compromise with the deficiencies and corruptions, and strive with greater vigor for the redemption of the world (more on this below 21:1).

It follows that the miracle is intended to reveal and publicize that God is the ruler of the entire world, and that it is fitting for all human beings to walk in His ways. The meaning of the word 'nes' (miracle) is a wonder, and also a banner raised aloft. The wondrous miracle is like a banner that is raised and lifted up to a great height so that it may be seen from afar, and through it people will know that God governs the world and all powers are in His hand. As it is stated (Tehillim 60:6): "You have given a banner (nes) to those who fear You, that it may be displayed because of the truth, Selah," that is, God gave those who fear Him a miracle in order to confirm and adorn [lit. "make true"] His words. Similarly, the meaning of the word 'ot' is both a sign and a wondrous marvel, as it is stated (Shemot 4:17): "And you shall take this staff in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs (otot)." For the sign is an indication of God's overall governance in the world.2

sections.title: The Great Miracles Are Essential for Israel
sections.html:
Above and beyond all the miracles stand the two great miracles through which God was revealed to the world, and by virtue of which the world exists: the Exodus from Egypt and the Giving of the Torah. Even if a person were to try with all his might to contemplate the divine light hidden in the laws of nature, without the miraculous revelation of the Giving of the Torah he would not merit clear divine guidance concerning faith and the path to the rectification of man and the world, and he would lose his way in the thicket of his troubles and aspirations. Likewise, the divine choice of the people of Israel to reveal His word to the world is the basis for receiving the Torah, and this choice was revealed in the miracles of the Exodus from Egypt.

Therefore, the choice of Israel and the Giving of the Torah took place with signs and wonders, so that all would know that they precede all the matters of the world, with all its laws of nature, because through Israel and the Torah God's governance in the world is revealed. This is what the Sages said: God could have taken Israel out with a single plague, or even through the way of nature, but in order to reveal to Israel and to the world His greatness and might, that there is no power that can stand before Him, He struck the Egyptians with ten plagues, until they submitted and sent Israel out to freedom. As it is stated (Shemot 7:3): "And I will multiply My signs and My wonders in the land of Egypt," and it is stated (Shemot 10:2): "And that you may tell in the ears of your son and of your son's son how I made a mockery of Egypt, and My signs which I have done among them, that you may know that I am the Lord." And even after Israel left Egypt, God hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he would pursue them, in order to save them through the great miracle of the splitting of the Red Sea, as it is stated (Shemot 14:4): "And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he shall pursue them, and I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his host, and Egypt shall know that I am the Lord." And it is stated (Shemot 14:31): "And Israel saw the great hand which the Lord had wielded against Egypt, and the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord and in Moshe His servant." Therefore we were commanded to remember the Exodus from Egypt every day, and on Shabbatot and festivals, in mezuzot and in tefillin, so that we remember the faith that was revealed in the miracles that God performed at the Exodus from Egypt (Ramban, Shemot 13:16).

Likewise, the Giving of the Torah took place before the eyes of all Israel with thunder and lightning and a supernal and awesome miraculous revelation, until the souls of Israel departed (Makkot 24a), and they could not continue to withstand the intensity of the revelation, and they asked that Moshe Rabbeinu tell them the rest of God's words, as it is stated (Shemot 20:16): "And they said to Moshe: You speak with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die" (above 16:10, note 7).

All these great and awesome miracles were intended to establish faith in God and in the destiny of Israel. As it is stated (Devarim 4:32-35): "For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man upon the earth, and from one end of heaven to the other, whether there has been anything like this great thing, or whether anything like it has been heard. Did a people ever hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and live? Or has God ever attempted to go and take for Himself a nation from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that the Lord your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes? To you it was shown, that you might know that the Lord, He is God; there is none else besides Him."

Also at the beginning of the campaign for the conquest of the Land, God performed great miracles for Israel: He split the Jordan before them, brought down the wall of Jericho, and made the sun stand still at Giv'on until Israel finished striking the five kings of the hill country. And although the essence of the mitzva was to conquer the Land through the ways of nature, God performed these miracles in order to make known to Israel and to all the inhabitants of the world that it is by the command of God that Israel enters the Land and conquers it.3

sections.title: The Transition to Governance through the Way of Nature
sections.html:
In the wilderness, Israel subsisted for forty years by way of miracle, nourished by the manna that came down from heaven, as it is stated (Devarim 8:3-4): "And He fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that He might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord does man live. Your garment did not wear out upon you, nor did your foot swell, these forty years." And in all their ways God guarded them and led them, as it is stated (Shemot 13:21-22): "And the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people."

However, after God had revealed Himself to Israel by way of miracle in the wilderness, the great hour arrived for Israel to begin revealing the word of God in the world through the ways of nature. Therefore, as a rule, from the time Israel entered the Land, the miracles ceased and they began to conduct themselves through the way of nature, and they had to be responsible for their own food, to plow and to sow, to plant and to prune, in order to grow with their own hands the holy fruits of the Land. Thereby they merited to fulfill the mitzva of settling the Land, which is equivalent to all the mitzvot of the Torah, and they began to sanctify the name of Heaven in the most exalted way. For when God is revealed only through miracle, the world is in darkness, and only the stars of the miracle shine from time to time. But when God is revealed through Israel walking in His ways through the ways of nature, the divine revelation fills the entire world, and it is revealed "that the Lord, He is God in heaven above and upon the earth beneath; there is none else" (Devarim 4:39). In heaven – through the Torah and the supernal revelations; and upon the earth – through man's choice to walk in the ways of God and to reveal His word and His blessing through the ways of nature.

The transition from the period of miracle to the period of nature resembles the course of a person's life: in his childhood his parents provide for all his needs, and as he grows up he becomes responsible for his own life and must provide for his livelihood himself, and if his parents were to continue feeding him and clothing him, it would be a disgrace for him. So too the people of Israel: in the first stage God provided for all their needs, like a mother caring for her nursing infant, and as Israel grew and matured, the responsibility passed to them, so that they would merit to reveal the word of God in the world through their choice and their actions (Ein Aya, Berakhot 1:143). Therefore Israel was commanded to conquer the Land through the ways of nature, and all the censuses that took place in the wilderness were censuses of those eligible for military service who had to conquer the Land. And in this the spies sinned, for they were afraid to take upon themselves the responsibility of conquering the Land through the way of nature.4

sections.title: The Combination of Miracle and Nature
sections.html:
The destiny of Israel is to settle the Land and to fulfill all the mitzvot of the Torah through the ways of nature; however, even when Israel walk in the ways of nature, they must remember the great miracles that God performed for them. Through this they will always remember God, the Creator of the world and its Ruler, by whose command they settle the Land in order to reveal His blessing to the world.

Like a person, who must remember the period when he was an infant and his parents fed him, clothed him and provided for all his needs, and through this, when he grows up, he will draw from his childhood memories the strength of spirit to be a good and responsible person, to establish a family and to add his contribution to society and to the nation. So too Israel must remember the great miracles that God performed for them when they went out of Egypt and in the wilderness, and from this they will draw strength of spirit to settle the Land through the ways of nature and to reveal the word of God and His blessing to the world.

This is what was said to Israel (Devarim 8:1-3): "All the commandment which I command you this day you shall observe to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land which the Lord swore to your fathers. And you shall remember all the way which the Lord your God led you these forty years in the wilderness…" And the Torah warned that if we do not remember God's miraculous providence over us in the wilderness, there is a concern that engaging in the settlement of the Land, which brings blessing and greatly empowers a person, will cause us to become arrogant and to forget God and the destiny incumbent upon us, as it is stated (ibid. 8:17): "And you say in your heart: My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth," and as a result we will perish from the good Land. So that this should not happen, the Torah instructed (ibid. 8:18): "But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is He who gives you power to get wealth, that He may establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers, as at this day."

The Ran noted the precise wording and explained that had the Torah wished to diminish the value of the work of Israel's hands, it would have said: 'for it is He who gives you wealth'; but it said "for it is He who gives you power to get wealth," to teach us that Israel produce the wealth by their own power, except that they must remember that God gave them this power (the Ran, beginning of derush 10).

The Land of Israel is the Holy Land, in which the word of God is revealed through natural reality. However, when Israel is in exile, since it is not possible to reveal the word of God within natural reality, holiness is revealed only through miracle above nature, and even the survival of Israel despite all the persecutions is by miracle. But this is a situation of be-di'avad (a less-than-ideal state), as our master Rav Kook ztz"l wrote (Orot Ha-teḥiya 28): "The holiness in nature is the holiness of the Land of Israel, and the Shekhina that went down into exile with Israel is the capacity to establish holiness in opposition to nature. But the holiness that fights against nature is not complete holiness."5

sections.title: The Crisis after the Miracle
sections.html:
Although miracles are needed to reveal God's power and His governance in the world, a miracle is generally followed by a crisis. For the path that God established for man's progress is through the way of nature, for in this manner he becomes accustomed to progressing by virtue of his diligence and resourcefulness, and to being saved from dangers by virtue of his caution. But when he merits blessing or rescue by way of miracle, a dangerous gap is created between his own condition and what he received through the miracle, and therefore his existence hangs by a thread, and everything he has may quickly be lost. Since he did not work with diligence and resourcefulness to earn the blessing, he does not know how to preserve the good he received and continue to progress. Since he did not learn to defend himself against dangers, the threats against him will grow. For example, a person who became wealthy gradually through his work and talent learned in the course of his work how to manage his money responsibly, but one who suddenly won a huge sum does not know how to handle it, and many times he errs and loses it. Likewise, a leader who grew gradually knows how to lead people and drive processes, but one who was suddenly chosen as leader many times errs and falls. So too a nation that won a war by way of miracle will likely be defeated in the next war, for its enemies will prepare well for war against it, whereas it does not know how to prepare a victorious army.

Therefore it is preferable for Israel not to rely on miracles, and if they needed miracles, they should exert themselves greatly through the ways of nature in order to be worthy of their situation without a miracle. However, in practice the miracle may overshadow nature, and therefore those who merit a miracle tend to despise the hard work in the way of nature that produces slow progress, and they mistakenly think that the proper level in God's eyes is that human beings pray to Him and hope for a miracle, and through small efforts merit great successes. Thus, instead of devoting themselves to the study of the Torah in all its parts, they will spend much time learning about the great miracles and marveling at them. Instead of devoting themselves to fulfilling all the mitzvot between man and God and between man and his fellow, they will be scrupulous about pious customs and neglect the other mitzvot. Instead of praying to God to help them be diligent in their work through the ways of nature, they will pray for a miracle, contrary to the guidance of the Sages, who warned not to rely on miracles.6

And so we find in the Tanakh that after a miracle a fall occurs, and the greater the miracle, the harsher the fall (see below, section 8). So too it happened to the generation that came out of Egypt: there was no generation that saw more miracles and wonders than it, but since it merited divine revelation through miracle without having risen by its own efforts in the study of faith, it failed in the sin of the golden calf; and since it was not accustomed to realizing the words of the Torah through the ways of nature, it failed in the sin of the spies, and it was decreed upon it to die in the wilderness. Not only that, but according to Rabbi Akiva the generation of the wilderness has no share in the World to Come; however, according to Rabbi Eliezer, despite their failure they have a share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 110b).

It follows that a miracle is like a loan at high interest; therefore, immediately after a person has merited a miracle he must gird himself with courage and humility, rectify himself through diligence and increase good deeds, so that he will be worthy of what he received as a gift through the miracle. But if he does not succeed, he will pay the price of the loan with interest. And only those who come after him will be able to be impressed by the miracle in a balanced way, and receive from it an illumination of faith that will not cause them to be lax in the work through the ways of nature.7

sections.title: Miracles in Times of Crisis
sections.html:
When Israel chooses the good, blessing flows through the way of nature, as we learned in the Torah: when one walks in God's statutes, the rain falls in its season and the land yields its produce, Israel grows strong and its enemies fall before it. Similarly, with the Patriarchs and Matriarchs we find almost no miracles; they walked in the ways of God, and God helped them. So too it was in the days of Shmuel, who taught the people to walk in the ways of God, and they merited victories over their enemies through the way of nature. And likewise in the days of David and Shlomo, they merited natural blessing and did not need miracles.

However, when Israel sins and its strength is weakened, it needs miracles. For the miracle is intended to make God's name known in the world, as with the miracles of the Exodus from Egypt, or to give help when there is no other way of rescue (Ramban, Devarim 20:9). Thus, in the days of the wicked kings who led Israel in the worship of the Ba'al, the prophets Eliyahu and Elisha arose, performed great miracles, and granted Israel a reprieve in which to repent. And although they did not repent, and the kingdom of Israel was destroyed and the Ten Tribes were exiled, an important legacy remained for Israel from the miracles: that God governs the world, and out of His love for Israel His people He sent them His prophets to try to save them. From this they knew that when they repent, God will redeem them.

So too, the great miracle of rescue performed for Ḥizkiyahu, king of Yehuda, pointed to the low state of Israel, while attempting to arouse them to repentance (Ein Aya, Berakhot 1:143). But since they did not repent, the process of destruction continued, and only the miracle remained as a testimony for Israel for the days of their exile: that if they cleave to the Torah, even if their exile is long, God will perform a miracle for them and protect them. As the Sages said (Sanhedrin 94a), by virtue of the Torah study that Ḥizkiyahu promoted, they were saved from Sanḥeriv. For Ḥizkiyahu would supply oil to the study halls so that they could light lamps and study Torah at night, until "they searched from Dan to Be'er Sheva and did not find an ignoramus." Ḥizkiyahu did err in rebelling against Assyria before he rectified the corruption of the officials and the sins between man and his fellow (Yeshayahu 1); however, since he increased Torah study, he merited to be saved by a miracle, and thereby bequeathed the legacy of survival through cleaving to Torah study for all the long and hard days of exile.

And so the Sages said (Mishna Sota 9:15) that after the Temple was destroyed we went down from one decline to another, there are no people of deeds among us and the men of force have prevailed, "and on whom can we rely? On our Father in heaven." Some mistakenly think that it is a merit that the people of Israel has no one to rely on except their Father in heaven. But the Sages meant to say that this is the nadir of the decline of the people of Israel, when they lack the strength to survive on their own, and they survive only by a miracle. Indeed, the survival of the people of Israel in the Diaspora is by a miracle, for in the way of nature a people exiled from its place assimilates into other peoples – all the more so when in its exile it is scattered and dispersed, continues to wander from land to land, and the various nations persecute it for its religion and for being different from them. The miracle of the survival of the Jewish people in exile did occur through the way of nature, but from a long-range view it is above and beyond ordinary miracles. And it was sustained through cleaving to the Torah and the mitzvot, through which Israel preserved their identity and their faith in the redemption.

Similarly, we find wonders that righteous people performed in the Diaspora to help private individuals in their time of trouble, and the harsher the situation, the more the stories of wonders multiplied. In contrast, the life of the people of Israel in the Land of Israel runs through the way of nature, in such a way that when they walk in the ways of God, divine blessing flows without the need for miracles.

sections.title: Four Kings
sections.html:
The Sages said (Eikha Rabba 4:15): "There were four kings; what this one requested, that one did not request. And they are: David, Asa, Yehoshafat and Ḥizkiyahu." King David prayed to God and asked: "I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are consumed" (Tehillim 18:38); that is, he asked that God help Israel strike a decisive blow against their enemies in a natural manner, and God helped him, and he struck all his enemies and laid the foundation for the kingdom of Yehuda and Israel for more than four hundred years.

About sixty years after the death of King David, Asa reigned in Yehuda, and when Zeraḥ the Kushite came up against him from Egypt with a very great army, he was afraid and prayed to God to help him by way of miracle. He said: "I have no strength to kill them; rather, I will pursue them and You kill them. And the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him and killed his enemies." However, afterward Asa did not succeed in continuing on the exalted path, and when Israel and Aram came up against him in war, instead of trusting in God, defeating them and reuniting the kingdom of Yehuda and Israel, he took all his treasures and the treasures of the Temple to bribe Aram to come over to his side and kill [the people of] Israel. And when the prophet rebuked him for this, he punished and humiliated him. He also oppressed and crushed the people. In the end he suffered for two years from a severe disease in his feet, and died.

Yehoshafat his son, who reigned after him, walked in the ways of God, but as a result of being drawn after the house of Aḥav, his army was struck and weakened, and when Moav, Amon and the people of Se'ir came up against him in war, he was very afraid, for he had no soldiers left to stand against them. However, Yehoshafat strengthened himself in faith and roused the people to sing a song to God and to pray for a miracle, and asked of God: "I have no strength either to kill or to pursue; rather, I will sing a song and You kill my enemies. And the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him and killed his enemies." While they were singing the song, a quarrel broke out in the enemy camp, and the three nations began fighting one another, until many of them died, and the remainder fled and left much spoil. It was a tremendous miracle, but the problems that led to the crisis that required the miracle were not rectified. As we learned, according to the magnitude of the miracle so is the magnitude of the calamity that is liable to come afterward. Within four years of Yehoshafat's death, all his offspring were destroyed by Atalya, and only one small son, named Yo'ash, survived, and from him the dynasty of the house of David continued (II Divrei Ha-yamim 20-22; II Melakhim 8:25-29; 11:1-3).

About a hundred and forty years after Yehoshafat, King Ḥizkiyahu reigned in Yehuda; he was one of the righteous among the kings. He abolished the idolatry that his father Aḥaz had set up in the Temple, and greatly strengthened the Temple service and Torah study, especially in the laws of ritual impurity and purity (Sanhedrin 94b). However, although the moral state of the officials and the people was still at a low ebb, he erred in rebelling against Assyria. The Assyrians came up against Yehuda and destroyed its cities, killed hundreds of thousands of Jews, and came up against Jerusalem to conquer it. The situation was desperate. Ḥizkiyahu cried out to God and said: "I have no strength either to kill, or to pursue, or to sing a song; rather, I will sleep in my bed and You act. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: I will act." At night the angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of Assyria, and the remainder returned in shame to Assyria (II Melakhim 18-19). There was no greater miracle of rescue than this; but, as we learned, according to the magnitude of the miracle so is the magnitude of the calamity that is due to come if they do not succeed in rectifying all that is needed. Ḥizkiyahu did try to rectify, but the rectification was not sufficient, and the prophet Yeshayahu was sent to inform him of the destruction and exile awaiting Yehuda and Israel, and that his descendants would be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. The actual destruction came more than a hundred years later, but it became clear that the miracle had not helped. Menashe, Ḥizkiyahu's son, who was born after the great miracle and by virtue of it, was more wicked than all the kings of Yehuda, and in his days the decree of destruction and exile upon Yehuda was sealed.

Once again we have learned that blessing that comes through the ways of nature by choosing the good is preferable to blessing that comes by way of miracle, as with King David: there was no king who prayed to God more than he, but his prayer was that God would give him strength to prepare his army and to defeat his enemies with his own hands. This is the exalted path for revealing faith, through which the divine idea is revealed through all the natural forces.8

sections.title: The Mitzvot Must Be Performed through the Way of Nature
sections.html:
The mitzvot must be performed through the way of nature, as the Ramban explained (Bamidbar 1:45), that this is why God commanded Moshe to count those eligible for military service in Israel in preparation for the war of conquest of the Land, "for the Torah does not rely on the miracle that one will pursue a thousand." Therefore they also had to send spies in preparation for the conquest of the Land, for one should not rely on a miracle but should fulfill the mitzva in the way of nature (Ramban, Bamidbar 13:2). For a miracle is performed in order to make known God's governance in the world, as happened at the Exodus from Egypt and the Giving of the Torah, or for the rescue of Israel when there is no other way. There is only one mitzva in which the Torah relies on a miracle, and that is the mitzva of testing the sota (a wife suspected of adultery) by means of the bitter waters (Ramban, Bamidbar 5:20), in order to teach us the great value of the sanctity of the family. And even this test was carried out in Israel only while they kept themselves in holiness and the Shekhina rested among them; but from the time adulterers multiplied, the sota waters ceased to test adulterous women (Sota 47a).

Similarly, the Sages said (Mishna Avot 5:5): "Ten miracles were performed for our forefathers in the Temple." Among them, that the sacrificial meat never became putrid. Nevertheless, they did not prepare tables of gold or silver for placing the meat, lest it become putrid; rather, they prepared tables of marble for this (Mishna Tamid 3:5; Rambam, Bartenura). Another miracle that occurred in the Temple was that the High Priest never had a seminal emission on the night of Yom Ha-kippurim; nevertheless, they made great efforts to keep him awake all night, for one does not rely on a miracle (Yerushalmi Yoma 1:4). They further said that by a miracle the showbread remained warm and fresh after a week (Yoma 21a), yet they took the trouble to place it in a manner that prevented it from becoming moldy (Yerushalmi Shekalim 6:3). Regarding the very fact that there were ten miracles in the Temple, the Maharal explained (Derekh Ḥayim there) that since the Temple is holy and separate from nature, it is necessary that there be miracles in it.

Even the great miracles, intended to reveal the word of God in the world, God took care to have them occur after an awakening on the part of Israel, so that they would be partners in bringing them about, and would not mistakenly think that their actions have no value. Therefore the Exodus from Egypt took place after Israel agreed to slaughter the idols of Egypt to God. And likewise the Sages said that the splitting of the Red Sea occurred after Naḥshon ben Aminadav began to enter the sea (Sota 37a). And likewise the Giving of the Torah came after Israel said: "All that the Lord has spoken we will do" (Shemot 19:8).

In prayer too, one prays for things that can come through the way of nature, and one does not request miracles. Therefore, even when water was greatly needed, they established fasts for prayer for rain only while there was still a chance that it would fall, up to half a month before the festival of Shavu'ot, and not after that, for then the falling of rain would be by way of miracle, and one does not pray "for a miraculous occurrence" (Yerushalmi Ta'anit 3:2). And likewise in all matters that a person needs, he should not pray that God perform for him a miracle outside the way of nature (Sefer Ḥasidim 794; Gevurat Ari, Ta'anit 19a).9

sections.title: Trust in God
sections.html:
Included in the mitzva of faith is that a person should trust in God that everything that happens to him is from God and for the good. And so it is stated: "Trust in the Lord forever, for in God the Lord is an everlasting Rock" (Yeshayahu 26:4); "Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust the Lord is" (Yirmeyahu 17:7); "Trust in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faithfulness" (Tehillim 37:3); "O Israel, trust in the Lord; He is their help and their shield" (ibid. 115:9).

The intent is not that a person should trust that God will always answer his requests, but rather that he should trust in God, who governs His world with justice, and that even the bad things that happen to him are for his good – sometimes in order to punish him and atone for his sins, and sometimes in order to test him and elevate him (see above 1:22). Therefore: "A person is obligated to bless [God] for the bad just as he blesses for the good" (Mishna Berakhot 9:5; SA OḤ 222:3). As it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might (me'odekha)" – the Sages expounded: "'With all your might' – with every measure (mida) that He metes out to you, thank Him (modeh) very, very much (bi-me'od me'od)." And likewise it is stated (Tehillim 56:11): "In God (Elokim) I will praise His word; in the Lord (Hashem) I will praise His word"; the Sages expounded (Berakhot 60b): "'In the Lord I will praise His word' – this is the attribute of good; 'In God I will praise His word' – this is the attribute of punishment." And as 'Naḥum Ish Gam Zu' was accustomed to say about every bad thing that happened to him: "This too is for the good" (Ta'anit 21a; below 21:5); and his disciple Rabbi Akiva also said: "A person should always be accustomed to say: Kol de-avid Raḥmana le-tav avid (everything that the Merciful One does, He does for the good)," and so he conducted himself (Berakhot 60b).

Included in the mitzva is that he should trust in God that He governs His world with justice: if he chooses the good, he will merit reward, and if he chooses evil, he will be punished – and this too is for his good, in order to refine him and arouse him to repent. And even if he does not repent and is punished in Gehinnom, this too is for the good, so that he will be refined and be able to ascend to Gan Eden. And even if he is among the wicked who are consumed in Gehinnom and whose souls become ashes under the soles of the feet of the righteous in Gan Eden (Rosh Hashana 17a), this too is for his good, for through this his corruptions will be removed from the world, and as a result he will ultimately merit to be revived (Rav Tzadok, Takanat Ha-shavin 15:76).

Indeed, the more he chooses the good, the more God will help him succeed, especially when he goes to fulfill a mitzva. And the greater the mitzva, the greater the importance of trust in God at the time of its fulfillment. Therefore, when the soldiers of Israel go out to fight the wars of God against their enemies, and thereby fulfill two of the most important mitzvot in the Torah – settling the Land and defending Israel from the hand of the enemy – the Torah commanded them not to be afraid but to trust in God, that by strengthening themselves in fulfilling the mitzva of war with resourcefulness and courage, they will defeat their enemies. As it is stated (Devarim 7:17-19): "If you say in your heart: These nations are more numerous than I; how can I dispossess them?! You shall not be afraid of them; you shall well remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt… so shall the Lord your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid." And it is stated (ibid. 20:1): "When you go out to battle against your enemies, and see horses and chariots, a people more numerous than you – you shall not be afraid of them, for the Lord your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."

However, when Israel sins, they are punished and their enemies defeat them, as is stated in the section of the curse (Vayikra 26:17): "And you shall be struck down before your enemies." Then, if they trust in God that despite their sins they will be victorious, this trust will have nothing to rely on, as happened in the days of Ḥizkiyahu, who erred in trusting in God and rebelling against Assyria, despite the moral nadir in the mitzvot between man and his fellow and the corruption of the officials. And likewise in the days of King Yoshiyahu, the prophet Yirmeyahu instructed him not to go out to war against the Egyptian army that was passing through the Land of Israel, because the sins of idolatry had not yet been properly rectified (Eikha Rabba 1:53). And Yoshiyahu, who thought he had already brought his generation back in proper repentance, trusted in God and went out to fight, and was defeated and died. And likewise in the days of King Tzidkiyahu, the false prophets called on the people to trust in God and rebel against Babylon, while Yirmeyahu prophesied in the name of God that they should not rebel; and in the end they rebelled and the Temple was destroyed.

In the absence of a prophet, the people of Israel must act according to the guidance of the Torah, which commanded going out to war to defend Israel from their enemies, and to inherit the Land when there is a reasonable chance of conquering it and defending it. Then it is a mitzva to strengthen oneself in trust in God, that since the soldiers are fulfilling a mitzva, God will help them defeat their enemies. And if, Heaven forfend, we are not worthy, we will know that failure too is for the good, so that we will make a soul-searching (ḥeshbon nefesh), and out of love for the people and the Land we will strengthen ourselves in Torah and mitzvot, until we defeat all our enemies and merit the redemption.10

sections.title: Effort and Trust
sections.html:
A person must work diligently to earn a livelihood through the ways of nature, and pray to God to send blessing upon all the work of his hands, as it is stated (Devarim 15:18): "And the Lord your God will bless you in all that you do." The Sages said (Sifrei there): "'And the Lord your God will bless you' – could it be [even when he is] idle? Therefore the verse states: 'in all that you do'." "If a person acts, he is blessed; and if not, he is not blessed" (Yalkut Shimoni, Devarim 808). And likewise, everywhere in the Torah where it says that if Israel keeps the mitzvot they will merit blessing, the intent is to blessing that comes through the way of nature, through a person's own activity. And likewise in the book of Mishlei, King Shlomo praises those who work diligently and condemns those who are lazy in their work (Mishlei 6:6, 9; 19:24; 22:13; 24:30, and elsewhere). That is to say, trust in God means that if one makes the effort to work with diligence and resourcefulness in order to add good and blessing to the world, God will help him.

Therefore, one who is lax and does not work for his livelihood sins against his family, and also sins in not fulfilling his destiny as a human being to engage in the settlement of the world (yishuvo shel olam), as it is stated (Bereshit 2:15): "to work it and to guard it." And since he sins, he will be punished in this world and in the World to Come. The simple punishment in this world is that he will be poor, and sometimes, out of his poverty, he will be tempted to commit further sins such as theft and fraud, and then his punishment will be more severe. And if he sins by not working out of an error in [understanding] the words of Torah, he will also desecrate God's name. As the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Talmud Torah 3:10), that one who lives off charity in order to study Torah "has desecrated the Name, disgraced the Torah, extinguished the light of religion, brought evil upon himself, and taken his life from the World to Come" (see Peninei Halakha: Likutim I 3:7).

Indeed, there were some of the great figures of Israel who emphasized more the value of trust (bitaḥon): that a person should trust in God that He will send him his sustenance, for a person's sustenance is allotted to him from Rosh Hashana to Rosh Hashana (Beitza 16a), and the need to work is because after the sin of Adam, God decreed upon man that he would not receive his livelihood without a certain effort (Mesillat Yesharim 21; Panim Me'irot, Devarim 8:17). However, it seems that their words were said concerning the temporary situation of Israel in the Diaspora, where in any case whatever they accumulate in the Diaspora would likely in the end be taken from them by their oppressors, and if it is not taken, it would cause them to become too settled in the exile. Therefore it is sufficient for them to make the effort needed for their subsistence, and thus, as soon as they are able to go up to the Land, it will not be hard for them to leave their property, and they will go up to the Land of Israel, where working for a livelihood is included in the mitzva of settling the Land (Ḥatam Sofer, Sukka 36a).

And one should not argue that since a person is engaged in Torah study or in a mitzva matter, he may rely on a miracle and be lax in [earning] his livelihood or in guarding himself from danger. For we find that even the great figures of Israel worked for their livelihood, such as Bo'az, who winnowed barley on the threshing floor (Rut 3:2). Likewise, a person is forbidden to rely on God to help him and save him from dangers; rather, he is commanded to guard himself from them (Shabbat 32a; Ta'anit 20b; Rambam, Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ U-shmirat Ha-nefesh 12:6; Rema, YD 116:5). Even one who goes to perform a great mitzva, when the danger is common, may not rely on God's help, but is obligated to strive as much as possible to reduce the danger. As we learned from Shmuel the prophet: after God commanded him to anoint David, he said to God: "How can I go? If Shaul hears, he will kill me!" And God instructed him to offer a sacrifice there, in order to conceal thereby the purpose of his coming, as it is stated: "Take a heifer with you, and say: I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. And invite Yishai to the sacrifice, and I will make known to you what you shall do, and you shall anoint for Me the one whom I name to you" (I Shmuel 16:2-3; Pesaḥim 8a).

sections.title: Redemption through the Way of Nature
sections.html:
The redemption of Israel, namely the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the Land, must take place through the way of nature. For the mitzva of immigrating to the Land and settling it is a practical mitzva that must be fulfilled by the whole of Israel, who must inherit the Land and apply Israeli sovereignty over it, and by each and every individual of Israel, who must live in the Land and engage in settling it (see Peninei Halakha: Ha-am Ve-ha-aretz 3:1-3). It follows that the sin that causes the delay of the redemption is the national laxity in organizing the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the Land, and the laxity of each individual of Israel in immigrating to the Land and settling in it.

And so we find in the second redemption, in the days of the return from Babylon and the building of the Second Temple, that the majority of Israel did not go up to the Land, and therefore the people of Israel did not succeed in attaining sovereignty over the Land, the Shekhina did not rest in the Temple, and we were not obligated in terumot, ma'asrot and shevi'it by Torah law (see Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 12:11). Therefore Reish Lakish said (Yoma 9b) that he hates the Babylonians who did not go up to the Land in the days of Ezra, for on their account the resting of the Shekhina in the Temple was partial, the settlement in the Land was weak, and in the end the Second Temple was destroyed and Israel went out again into a long exile.

From this exile too Israel must be redeemed through the way of nature. For God commanded Israel to settle the Land through the way of nature. And the more they engage in this mitzva, the faster and less painful their redemption will be. Concerning this the Sages said (Sanhedrin 98a) that if Israel is worthy, the redemption will come quickly and gently, in the manner of 'aḥishena' ("I will hasten it"). That is, out of an awakening of faith, men of spirit and of action will unite to find the ways to ingather the exiles and settle the Land, taking into account all the political, social and economic difficulties, for the mitzva of settling the Land is a mitzva that must be fulfilled within concrete reality (see Peninei Halakha: Zemanim 4:4).

But if they are not worthy, the redemption will come after a long time and with great suffering, in the manner called 'be-itah' ("in its time"). That is to say, out of the terrible hardships that will keep intensifying in the Diaspora, Jews will flee to their Land, and from crisis to crisis they will advance in the settlement of the Land, until in the end they will also return to the Torah and the mitzvot. As the Sages said (Sanhedrin 97b), the redemption may come after "the Holy One, blessed be He, sets up over them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, and Israel repents and returns to the right path."

And it is possible that the redemption will come through a combination of 'be-itah aḥishena' ("in its time, I will hasten it"), as the Gra held would happen (Kol Ha-tor 1:8). And so indeed it happened in recent generations: out of a combination of decrees that kept intensifying together with an awakening to fulfill the mitzva of settling the Land, Jews began to immigrate to the Land in order to build it, and the Yishuv kept growing, until the Zionist movement arose, which began to act also through diplomatic means to obtain support from the nations of the world for the establishment of the State of Israel. And afterward, in the wake of the Holocaust, the Jewish people awoke to understand that the State of Israel must be established. And thus we keep advancing in the wake of crises and challenges. Our master Rav Kook wrote (Shemoneh Kevatzim 7:201): "They ask: By what merit did our generation merit the redemption? The answer is simple: it merited it because it engaged in the greatest mitzva of all the mitzvot, in the mitzva that is equivalent to the entire Torah, because it engaged in the redemption of Israel. And not only did it engage in it, but it engages and will engage unceasingly in its redemption, and this divine power elevates it and exalts it in salvation."11

sections.title: The Debate over a Natural Redemption
sections.html:
Some argue that although it is true that the essence of the redemption is the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the Land, these must come from God with signs and wonders. And they derived this from the plain sense of the verses, that it is God who will gather the exiles and settle the Land, as it is stated (Devarim 30:3-5): "Then the Lord your God will bring back your captivity and have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples to which the Lord your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are at the ends of the heavens, from there the Lord your God will gather you, and from there He will take you. And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; and He will do you good and multiply you more than your fathers." And likewise it is stated (Yeḥezkel 36:24): "For I will take you from among the nations, and gather you out of all the countries, and will bring you into your own land." And likewise in further verses in the Torah and the Prophets.

However, the intent of the Torah is that God will help Israel to fulfill the mitzva, for without God's help no human effort will bear fruit. As we bless God over bread: "Who brings forth bread from the earth" (Ha-motzi leḥem min ha-aretz) – yet it is man who toils over the bread, in plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, winnowing, sorting, grinding, kneading and baking! But since God created the earth and man, the wheat and the properties that make it possible to produce bread from it, God is considered the One "who brings forth bread from the earth." Thus a person must always remember that it is God who gave us the ability to understand and to act, and our role is to settle the Land through the ways of nature with the powers that God gave us. And if we do not explain it thus, we will, Heaven forfend, nullify the mitzva that God commanded Israel to settle the Land, as it is stated (Bamidbar 33:53-54): "And you shall take possession of the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it. And you shall inherit the land…" And it is stated (Devarim 11:31): "And you shall possess it and dwell in it."

And so wrote Rav Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer in his book 'Derishat Tziyon' (ma'amar 1): "The redemption of Israel for which we wait – let no one think that suddenly God, blessed be His Name, will descend from heaven to earth to say to His people: Go forth! Or that He will send His Mashiaḥ in an instant from heaven to sound a great shofar for the dispersed of Israel and gather them to Jerusalem, and make for it a wall of fire, and a Temple of God will descend from on high…." Rather, the redemption will come through Israel being aroused to immigrate to the Land and settle it, and as a result all the words of the prophets will be fulfilled in us.

And likewise we find that many of the sages of Israel, headed by Rabbi Akiva, hoped that Bar Kokhba would be the Mashiaḥ; and if the redemption depended on miracles, it would have been inconceivable that Bar Kokhba would be the Mashiaḥ, for all his activity for the independence of Israel was through the ways of nature. And so wrote the Rambam (Hilkhot Melakhim 11:3): "Do not imagine that the King Mashiaḥ must perform signs and wonders and bring about new things in the world, or revive the dead, and the like, as the fools say. It is not so; for Rabbi Akiva was a great sage among the sages of the Mishna, and he was the arms-bearer of Koziba the king, and he would say of him that he is the King Mashiaḥ; and he and all the sages of his generation imagined that he was the King Mashiaḥ, until he was killed because of sins. Once he was killed, it became known that he was not the Mashiaḥ. And the Sages did not ask him for a sign or a wonder."12

sections.title: The Process of Repentance and Redemption
sections.html:
From studying the words of the Torah, as Rav Tzvi Yehuda taught, we learn that the process of redemption will unfold such that at first Israel will return to their Jewish identity, immigrate to the Land and settle it, and this is called "and you shall return unto (ad) the Lord your God" – and 'ad' is not inclusive [i.e., up to but not yet fully reaching] – and from this they will continue to advance until they return in complete repentance "to (el) the Lord your God." As it is stated in Parashat Nitzavim (Devarim 30:1-10): "And it shall come to pass, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse which I have set before you, and you take it to heart among all the nations to which the Lord your God has driven you, and you return unto the Lord your God (to Jewish identity), and hearken to His voice (awakening to return to the Land of Israel and settle it) according to all that I command you this day, you and your children, with all your heart and with all your soul; then the Lord your God will bring back your captivity and have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples to which the Lord your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are at the ends of the heavens, from there the Lord your God will gather you, and from there He will take you. And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; and He will do you good and multiply you more than your fathers. (From this a process of spiritual repentance will begin.) And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. (From this we will merit great victories over our enemies.) And the Lord your God will put all these curses upon your enemies and upon those who hate you, who persecuted you. (From this we will continue to return more to the fulfillment of all the mitzvot.) And you shall return and hearken to the voice of the Lord, and do all His commandments which I command you this day. (And we will merit additional blessing.) And the Lord your God will make you abound in all the work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb, and in the fruit of your cattle, and in the fruit of your land, for good; for the Lord will again rejoice over you for good, as He rejoiced over your fathers. (All this by virtue of our returning to God in complete repentance.) When you hearken to the voice of the Lord your God, to keep His commandments and His statutes which are written in this book of the Torah, when you return to the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul."

And likewise we learn in Yeḥezkel (36:24-28) that even if Israel do not repent, it will not be possible to continue forever the desecration of God's name that persists throughout all the days of their exile, as the nations say: If the Lord is God, how can it be that His people is humiliated and oppressed and His Land desolate? Therefore: "For I will take you from among the nations, and gather you out of all the countries, and will bring you into your own land." And afterward God will arouse Israel to return to Him: "And I will sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall be pure; from all your impurities and from all your idols I will purify you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My spirit within you, and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you shall keep My ordinances and do them. And you shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers, and you shall be My people, and I will be your God."13

sections.title: Sanctification of God's Name through the Way of Nature and through Miracle
sections.html:
Some argue that the redemption must sanctify the name of Heaven, and that if it is through the way of nature there will be no sanctification of God's name in it, for only through signs and wonders will His name be sanctified. But the truth is that the great sanctification of God's name is when the children of Israel walk in the ways of God, and God blesses the work of their hands through the way of nature, as explained in the Torah (the sections of Beḥukotai and Ki Tavo). For then heaven and earth are joined, God's blessing flows in everything, all of creation sings, and it is revealed "that the Lord, He is God in heaven above and upon the earth beneath; there is none else" (Devarim 4:39). As Rabbi David Tevele wrote (Naḥalat David, derush 1), that when God governs the world in a hidden way under the wings of nature, this is the governance that "surpasses them all… when He sends the blessing upon the work of their hands… as was the case in the wars of David," and in this there was a greater sanctification of God's name than in the miracle that God performed for Ḥizkiyahu in his war against Sanḥeriv. Therefore King David did not ask God to perform a miracle for him. "For King David, peace be upon him, estimated in his soul that he was ready and destined to be a chariot for receiving the divine flow (shefa), even in his material limbs, arteries and sinews… and the desire was that he himself would be the one to strike them, and this is the greatest of the levels…."

Two explanations have been given for the fact that the prophets described the redemption as miraculous (Yeshayahu 11:1-10; 30:25-26; Yeḥezkel 38:18-23, and elsewhere), and both are true. The first is that it is meant to explain that God will help Israel succeed in immigrating to the Land and settling it (as explained in halakha 13). And the miraculous aspect in the descriptions is said in the language of parable, in order to describe the great wonder of the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the Land, which was desolate and ruined and will be transformed into a flourishing and thriving land – something that has never happened to any nation or any land. And likewise what is said, that the wolf will dwell with the lamb, means that the wicked of the world, who are compared to wolves, will not do evil by killing (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 12:1).

The second is that the miraculous descriptions were said concerning the World to Come, which follows the days of the Mashiaḥ and the redemption, which is indeed above and beyond the nature of this world and is entirely a miracle for us. This is what the Sages said (Sanhedrin 99a): "There is no difference between this world and the days of the Mashiaḥ except subjugation to the kingdoms alone"; thus even in the days of the redemption the world follows its usual course, except that Israel are free people in their Land and can choose the good, and only afterward, in the World to Come, will all of nature be perfected and elevated.

Indeed, at times we find in the words of Rishonim and Aḥaronim who wrote that the imminent redemption would take place by way of miracle, contrary to the mitzva of settling the Land, which, as we have learned, is a practical mitzva that must be fulfilled through the way of nature, and contrary to the destiny of Israel to reveal the word of God through the ways of nature. Perhaps they feared that Israel would despair of their redemption, after it seemed, ostensibly, that there was no chance of acting for the ingathering of the exiles and the settlement of the Land, and therefore they encouraged their spirits with hope for a miraculous redemption above nature. And there is truth in this, for even when the redemption comes out of suffering and through the way of nature, it has an aspect of an unbelievable miracle. However, just as miraculous help resembles a loan at high interest (above, halakha 6), so the encouragement given to Israel through the miraculous descriptions of the redemption is like a loan at interest, for which the payment is very high. For because of all the talk of a miraculous redemption, the mitzva to do everything to immigrate to the Land and settle it was forgotten, and so, when it was possible to immigrate to the Land, they remained in exile, and great and terrible troubles befell us: the Holocaust, the evil Communist regime, and assimilation. Perhaps there was no choice, and without the hope of a miracle we would not have survived; but the price of relying on the miracle was unbearably heavy.14

sections.title: Divine Blessing through the Ways of Nature
sections.html:
Let us describe the blessing and redemption that can come in our days through the way of nature, by walking in the ways of God. Out of recognition of the value of the Torah and of Israel, the people of Israel will grow stronger in faith and in the desire to add blessing to the world, and many Jews will immigrate to the Land. Out of understanding the value of the sanctity of the family, many will marry with joy and love, and raise many children in nurturing homes. By virtue of the desire to fulfill the mitzva of settling the Land, the Land of Israel will be built throughout its length and breadth. By virtue of the desire to fulfill the mitzva of enlisting in the army, the security situation of the State of Israel will improve. By virtue of the value of learning, many will invest more years in the professional studies that suit them, and the quality of their work will improve. Out of recognition of the value of science, many will reach good academic achievements, and groundbreaking scientists will arise in Israel. By virtue of recognizing the value of work and of contributing to the settlement of the world, workers will be happy in their work and work diligently. By virtue of the values of honesty and truth, investors and merchants will be more honest, and it will be more worthwhile to do business in Israel and to forge partnerships for the development of society and the economy. By virtue of Torah study on Shabbatot and festivals, and by setting times [for Torah] on weekdays, they will constantly be strengthened in all these values, and will merit more inspiration in development and creativity in all their deeds. Out of resting on Shabbatot and festivals, the festive prayers and the good meals in the bosom of the family, they will be strengthened in the values of faith and kindness. As a result, many will strive to develop ways and means to help those who are disabled and injured in body and soul, and the talent of all those which has been silenced because of various disabilities will be revealed and will make a new and original contribution to society. By virtue of the connection to the values of the Torah and morality, the people will choose good and upright leaders, who will lead Israel to the realization of all the values of the Torah.

By virtue of all this good, an exemplary, flourishing society will arise. The annual GDP of the State of Israel will grow more than that of the other developed countries. Scientific development for the benefit of humanity will advance more than in the other developed countries. The blessed demographic growth will continue consistently, and the people of Israel dwelling in its Land will number tens of millions, and will lead the world in values, science and economics. As a result, all the Jews remaining in the Diaspora will long to immigrate and join the success, and even the descendants of Israel who were lost to us under the pressure of the sufferings of the exiles will seek to clarify their roots and return to their people and their Land. And a great, mighty and numerous people will herald faith and justice to the world, will pave the way for moral education and intellectual development for the benefit of humanity, and will devise new methods and technologies for longevity and quality of life. As the Sages said (Berakhot 34b): "There is no difference between this world and the days of the Mashiaḥ except subjugation to the kingdoms alone." That is to say, in a natural way, in the light of the faith of Israel, human beings will choose the good and eradicate wickedness, and no one will subjugate his fellow, and all human talents will be channeled toward adding good and blessing. And the words of prophecy will be fulfilled in us (Yeshayahu 2:2-4): "And it shall come to pass in the end of days that the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established at the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it. And many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Yaakov, and He will teach us of His ways, and we will walk in His paths; for out of Zion shall go forth Torah, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."15
